walkthroughs.body_html:
Priestley's opening: "pink and intimate" lighting becomes "brighter and harder" when the Inspector arrives.

The lighting symbolises the Birlings' cosy denial being exposed by harsh truth.

walkthroughs.h2: The conch in Lord of the Flies
walkthroughs.body_html:
The conch is a symbol of order and democracy. When it shatters, civilisation collapses.

The boys' island is a microcosm of society — what happens there shows what could happen anywhere.

The Inspector's final speech ("We are members of one body") is Priestley's own mouthpiece for socialism.

Always link a character's words back to the writer's purpose.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Foreshadowing is the shadow a character casts in a scene.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
Foreshadowing is when a character predicts the future.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Foreshadowing is the shadow a character casts in a scene.
Subtle hints or clues earlier in a text that anticipate later events, making the resolution feel both surprising and inevitable.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: Foreshadowing is the shadow a character casts in a scene.
A theme is the title of the book.
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.
A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
